Photograph: Terje Pedersen/EPA View image in fullscreen The coffin of King Harald is taken to the royal mausoleum in the crypt at Akershus Castle after the funeral ceremony in Oslo. Photograph: Terje Pedersen/EPA Norway Tens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald V Europe’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a close Europe live – latest updates Jon Henley Europe correspondent Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Norway has observed a minute’s silence as it takes leave of King Harald V in a series of ceremonies, bringing to a close 13 days of ​national mourning that followed the popular monarch’s death last month at the age of 89. Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo and foreign heads of state and government converged on the Norwegian capital for the funeral of the late king, a light-touch and unassuming reformer who ruled for more than three decades. With the king’s casket carried on an artillery carriage, draped in Norway’s red royal banner and topped with white flowers, the funeral cortege made its way on foot along Oslo’s main avenue from royal palace to the cathedral, as a 21-gun salute rang out from the Akershus fortress. View image in fullscreen Norway’s Prince Sverre Magnus, King Haakon VIII, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Princess Martha Louise walk behind the coffin of King Harald V. Photograph: Ole Berg-Rusten/EPA King Haakon VIII, who succeeded his father on Harald’s death, and other royal family members walked behind the coffin, with Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, 89, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, following in a car. View image in fullscreen Despite its recent scandals, the monarchy remains broadly popular. Photograph: Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix/AP The procession was followed by a church ceremony attended by royals including the Britain’s Prince William and Princess Anne; Spain’s King Felipe and Queen Letizia; ‌Sweden’s royal family; Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary; the Netherlands’ King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima; and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and political leaders and dignitaries from more than 20 countries were at the service, at which the speaker of Norway’s parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, recalled a monarch who was “not afraid to meet his people with his rubber boots on”. View image in fullscreen The Prince of Wales and Princess Anne leaving the funeral service. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters The prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said Harald “struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth. He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.” After the service four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral, one breaking away to symbolise the king’s passing. The casket was then carried to the Akershus fortress where it was due to be lowered into the royal crypt, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents, in a private ceremony. View image in fullscreen A painted portrait of Norway’s King Harald V is displayed among flowers and Norwegian flags at a makeshift memorial outside the royal palace in Oslo. Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images Norwegian police said securing the funeral had been the largest planned operation in the force’s history. More than 46,000 Norwegians have filed past the king’s casket in the past week and schoolchildren were allowed to miss ⁠classes for the occasion. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Harald’s death came at a time of numerous crises for the Norwegian royal family, with Mette-Marit, 53, in particular coming under heavy criticism – including from the prime minister – for her association with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. View image in fullscreen Marius Borg Høiby leaves the funeral service. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters The new queen’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle monitor pending his appeal against a conviction for rape and domestic violence, was given permission to attend the funeral and was a pall-bearer during the transfer of Harald’s coffin to the royal chapel. Despite its recent scandals, however, the monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, according to a poll for the public broadcaster NRK. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/influence.text: Shaun Wilson Sat, August 29, 2026 at 11:23 PM UTC 1 An influencer broke down in tears in court as he denied helping to rob a fashion designer of his diamond-encrusted watch in central London. Abdel El Habchi, 30, who has around a million followers on Facebook, and Ali Eldahouzze, 22, are accused of robbing designer Catalin Botezatu. Jurors were told a third man, Younes Djoudi, has pleaded guilty to robbery. Mr Botezatu, who is a Romanian entrepreneur, had been having dinner with his assistant and a friend before he was allegedly robbed of his Richard Mille watch worth more than £137,000 by the trio, Southwark Crown Court heard. Giving evidence on Friday, El Habchi told jurors through an Arabic interpreter: “I had no idea it was going to happen, I did not participate, I didn’t know even that a watch was snatched or stolen until later on.” The court heard Mr Botezatu had been smoking a cigar with a friend on the terrace of Latin American restaurant Amazonico in Berkeley Square on the evening of January 28. Prosecutors allege that the watch was later cut from his wrist shortly before midnight. El Habchi, who grew up in a town near Casablanca, Morocco, told the court he came to the UK in 2019 on a spouse visa and is married with two children. Jurors heard that El Habchi had been working as a security guard, but also has a Facebook following of around a million, around 350,000 Instagram followers and a TikTok account. The defendant said he and his friend, Eldahouzze, had been travelling from Slough to Soho, central London, hours before the alleged robbery when Eldahouzze received a call from Djoudi telling him to meet in Mayfair. El Habchi told jurors that while in Djoudi’s car close to the restaurant, he sat in the back watching TikTok videos and heard Djoudi being “threatening” and aggressive towards Eldahouzze. While walking around the area later on, he saw Djoudi “use his hand to grab something from the hand” of a man, the court heard. Explaining why he ran from the scene, El Habchi said: “At that moment it was panic and after one or two seconds when I see Ali run I was panicked and I was completely lost, I had never been in this situation before.” El Habchi said that Eldahouzze later told him that Djoudi had threatened him to “execute what he asked him to do”. Asked by his barrister, Loheswaran Amirthananthar, how he felt at the time, El Habchi replied: “To be honest with you I felt as if I was betrayed, I had no idea what was happening and I found myself in this problem.” He said Eldahouzze told him he was “scared” of Djoudi. El Habchi told jurors that Djoudi met the pair the following morning with the watch. Asked whether any threats had been made against him, El Habchi tearfully replied: “He turned to me and made a threat ‘if you report anything to the police I will burn your kids’.” He said he was “under threat” and “scared” of Djoudi, who he claimed “has a lot of connections”. He added: “I was just concentrating on my kids’ safety. I was really scared and I find myself in the middle of a deep problem.” The court heard that all three men were incarcerated at Wandsworth prison after their arrests. El Habchi said that in April he was attacked by around 16 people in the prison and that Djoudi had “instigated” the assault. He told jurors he suffered a cut to his back and was stamped on the head. Prosecutor Arizuna Asante told the court on Tuesday that after leaving the restaurant, Mr Botezatu “stood near the car smoking for a few minutes with his friend before he was approached by three males”. Mr Asante told jurors: “The three males surrounded Mr Botezatu and robbed him of his watch by wresting it from his left wrist. “It is believed a knife was used to cut through the rubber strap because the victim had cuts on his wrists after the watch was taken.” Mr Asante, cross-examining El Habchi on Friday afternoon, said: “I’m going to suggest to you Mr El Habchi, that your intention in going to Berkeley Square was to see if there was anybody there with a high-value watch to steal or rob from them?” The defendant replied: “No.” The prosecutor added: “That’s why, isn’t it, that you, Mr Djoudi and Mr Eldahouzze walked up and down Amazonico eyeing Mr Botezatu as a target?” El Habchi replied: “I have no idea about this no.” Prosecutors say the watch would now be worth “significantly more” than 160,000 euro. El Habchi and Eldahouzze each deny one count of robbery. The trial continues.
